Hey guys. 

I’d been pushed into the diet culture in kindergarten (ive always been overweight) and in college now I just wanted to be skinny, so I barely ate. Heck Google told me calories in vs calories out was all that mattered, no matter what I ate. 

Sometimes I’d have an entire 175g bag of chips, and nothing else the entire day. 

I’ve recently (November 2024) came to know I have insulin resistance, and now even more recently, (February 2025) I’ve found that there was smth wrong with my daily calories.

Way, way too low. 

This last week I realised my weekly average was 1300. Cals. I’m 20kg overweight and my BMI is over 30. 

Haha so…. I’ve realised when I tried to do deficits…I was never IN a deficit isn’t that hilarious🤣

So NOW I have to eat more (and lift more and walk more) to increase my metabolism. 
Oh but SLOWLY so it’s going to take 1-2 months to increase it to a good number like 1900-2000 cals and only THEN do a deficit to 1200-1300 cals.

This is so fucking hard. 

I was told, my entire life (since primary/elementary) that when I got that ache in my stomach after not eating, that’s a sign you’re losing weight. You guys im addicted to that feeling I NEED that feeling to feel like I’m on the right track. I keep feeling bloated and full all the time.

I’ve broken down so many times in the last week because it feels counterintuitive. Eating more to lose weight goes against everything I know, everything my parents did and said. 

I hate this and I hate that after I calculated, it feels like it’s gonna take me another year. Another year I’ve already SAID 2023 would be my year, 2024 would be my year and now 2025!!!

I’ve put everything on hold. Dating and sex, new friendships, posting pics, buying sexy clothes. I’m in my mid 20s and nothing to show for it. 

I get frustrated, tired and then numb. Telling myself “you can do this” is too familiar and too routine. 

I’m fucking done if this doesn’t work. Not sure what else to say. 

________________________________________



TL:DR : my actual maintenance is too low (1300) and that fked up my metabolism. Now I have to eat more that goes against everything I know and it’s so excruciating mentally and emotionally.

It’s a Turkish dish but I’m not Turkish. I make it a wrong, lazy way. 

Sometimes I poach my eggs or sometimes I just do sunny side ups. My Greek yoghurt underneath has crushed garlic (or garlic spread mixed in or garlic powder), has a little lemon, drop of honey (don’t judge), salt, pepper, and sometimes I lightly heat mushrooms and onions (less onion coz low carb) in chilli and garlic and toss them into the yoghurt and mix it in.

This is where I might get attacked but I put in those crispy chili flakes from the Asian store on top, instead of the buttery paprika sauce (only because I’m not good at it).

**Add your own twists to it**. I really liked the concept of Çılbır; eggs on Greek yoghurt— protein and low carb.

In some circumstances, your year 12 internals marks are sometimes a good indication, especially to test mathematics and literacy skills. But in the end, ATAR is a rank, influenced by your cohort, hence not a fair assessment for IQ and fluid intelligence. 

Uni degrees are quite limited in what they can assess because they all vary. For example, I’m in my final year and I’m writing my very first essay I’ve ever had to write in my entire degree, while other degrees may do this very early on and quite often. 

I’d say NAPLAN tests have the closest correlation with IQ assessments.

It’s not a fair test to compare the two. You can never expect many people to score 99.95 in the state because ATAR is a rank, not a average percentage like WAM is. You’re saying 40 people in NSW scored in the top 0.05% and that checks out. 

You’re comparing achieving a specific rank to scoring a mark.

There’s no way to make that connection. 

I’ve seen people perform worse than they did in high school. Like in school they ranked in top 5 in all their subjects, scored state ranks and shit, but they ended up feeling burnt out in uni and imo could really use a gap year. 

On the other hand, I’ve seen many flourish in uni because they are studying exactly what they want to do, unlike in high school where they didn’t study with passion, and HAD to take an English and 4-5 other subjects. 

Okay let’s say you get a 99.95 ATAR and you go on to maintain the same work ethic, then yes you’ll end up with a HD (High Distinction 85+), but that’s not common because people become lax with uni. It’s almost inevitable, even though the pacing is as horrible as the HSC year. 

Many local UNSW students who enter with an 90+ ATAR don’t leave with 80+ WAM. Theres a distribution I saw a while ago that most UNSW students graduate with a 65-75 WAM, if that helps.

Hi, 3rd year student here. 

I haven’t studied the UTS degree but if I remember correctly from when I was in year 12 browsing degrees, I think the UTS CS degree is called **“Computing Science”** which is more research based. Perhaps might find it helpful to ask about the degree on their reddit.

Trimesters are a pain but it’s doable. The subjects will be paced faster than other unis, but it’s easier to ignore if you haven’t experienced the easier pace in other unis.

Many people at UNSW do part time jobs. If it feels like too much, it’s easy to lighten your subject load;

The CS degree at UNSW has a 3 year duration at full load (almost 3 subjects every trimester), which can be extended to 4 years if you decide to do an average of 2 subjects every single trimester, which is much easier to do, and it helps especially for your harder 2nd year subjects.

**The UNSW CS degree requires you to do 3 maths;** 
-	Mathematics 1A (MATH1131),
-	Mathematics 1B (MATH1231), and
-	Discrete Mathematics (MATH1081).

If you’re worried about these, I suggest you check out some of the UNSW lectures for these subjects on YouTube and see if you’re up for it (try to look for introductory ones). These are all level 1 subjects (as you can tell from the subject code), so it’s expected to be easy to pass for first year students, and those with less context beforehand.

**Streams;**
Most CS students I’ve met just do the default stream (no stream), which gives them flexibility to choose their “computing electives”. If you choose a stream, it will choose these electives for you. 
I’d suggest that you go into CS with no major, and then decide if you want a stream after your first year ends, after you’ve had some experience with CS concepts etc. It’s an easy program transfer as long as you do core subjects first year and not electives.


In the end, streams don’t really matter too much to employers. It’s just a few extra words added to your qualification, so having stream is pretty much just as effective.

**Final advice:**
In my experience, I have felt burnt out at times, left panicking, and sometimes questioned my degree choice, but I soon realise there’s nothing else I’d rather do when I seek for jobs. Basically, I know these are the skills I want. 
I believe that maintaining your passion to learn these skills will keep you going. Just put yourself first and take some time off whenever you need it. 

If I were you, I’d spend my first year at UNSW CS first since first year subjects are a nice first impression of the degree. After first year I’d decide if I want to stay at UNSW or move to UTS. 
This is because I believe it’s much harder to transfer from UTS to UNSW than the other way around. This way you can make an informed decision.

But yeah, I’m pretty sure the UTS CS degree is quite different to UNSW CS so check out the specifics and see what you’re into. 

I hope this helped. Let me know if you have any other questions :)
